claims.text: Introducing coherent nanoprecipitates into an HEA intermediate layer will improve its heat-transfer capability.
Introducing coherent nanoprecipitates will preserve the intermediate layer's mechanical strength under plasma-facing reactor conditions.
The starting intermediate layer is a single-phase HEA with a moderately coarse microstructure.
Current HEA intermediate-layer designs have moderate thermal conductivity.
Tailored thermal processing can induce stepwise-controllable coherent nanoprecipitation in an HEA matrix.
Adjustment of laser-cladding parameters can induce a uniform population of coherent nanoprecipitates in the proposed intermediate layer.
Plasma-facing reactor intermediate layers experience high thermal flux, temperatures up to approximately 1000°C, and cyclic thermomechanical loading.
The processing intervention will create finely and uniformly dispersed coherent precipitate phases in the HEA matrix.
Coherent matrix-precipitate interfaces provide efficient channels for heat conduction.
The coherent nanoprecipitates act as barriers against dislocation movement.
Coherent nanoprecipitation reduces phonon scattering at matrix-precipitate boundaries.
Reduced phonon scattering at coherent boundaries increases thermal conductivity.
Coherent interfaces reduce stress concentrations and resistance to premature crack initiation, thereby helping preserve mechanical integrity.
The treated intermediate layer will have approximately 10–20% higher thermal conductivity than the baseline.
The treated layer will retain strength and stability during high-temperature and cyclic loading.
Current single-phase HEA intermediate layers rely solely on bulk solid-solution properties for structural integrity.
Excessive precipitate formation may embrittle the intermediate layer.
The beneficial effects are likely restricted to a particular precipitate-volume-fraction range.
The nanoprecipitate distribution may lose stability during prolonged thermal cycling and thereby compromise integrity.
